idiom_name: parent struct owns the state; children attach through constructor functions
implementation_notes: Go has no widget tree in the standard library and no ambient scope, so the pattern is built by hand: a parent struct owns the value plus a slice of child handles, and constructor functions attach a child to its parent and return it - the equivalent of what retained-mode toolkits such as Fyne express with explicit container constructors (container.NewVBox and friends) rather than an implicit parent lookup. What replaces the classic structure is ordinary struct composition plus a registration call, and the child handles it stores are what the parent iterates to enforce the invariant. There is no change-notification machinery at all, so the parent must also own the redraw hook; where only two or three values are involved, passing them explicitly through fields or parameters stays clearer than a hidden channel.
pitfalls: Storing child handles in a slice that is appended to while children hold pointers is fine, but copying the parent struct by value into a child breaks the shared state - always share the pointer.
Re-slicing during registration can invalidate a snapshot of items another goroutine is iterating; keep the child set immutable after construction or guard it with a mutex.
Nothing re-renders on its own: without a callback or channel the UI shows the stale selection indefinitely.
Embedding the parent struct in the child type shares the parent's fields by copy, which looks like the pattern but silently gives each child its own state.
